_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 4 Science unit lecture film, Lesson 11 Inside the Earth. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. Every beat is one narration clip; art.at names the phrases a picture waits for, and the page refuses to load if a phrase is not in its beat's say. The chapters follow LESSON['lecture'] in order (three layers; volcanoes; earthquakes; a model to scale; how we know), in the lesson's own words: its tap figure (ART.figure earthLayers, one layer named at a time), its volcano demo (ART.scene volcano 0-3), its earthquake demo (ART.scene quake 0-3), the apple of its scale-model step, and the evidence of its 'How we found out' step.
title: Inside the Earth
subtitle: Grade 4 Science
objectives: Describe the model of the structure of the Earth which includes a core, a mantle and a crust.
Describe common features of volcanoes and know they are found at breaks in the Earth's crust.
Know that the Earth's crust moves and when parts move suddenly this is called an earthquake.
Know that models are not fully representative of a real world situation and/or scientific idea.
Use models to show relationships, quantities or scale.
Describe how scientific knowledge and understanding changes over time through the use of evidence gained by enquiry.

beats.say: Cut the Earth open, and you would find three layers.
Nobody has ever dug down to see them. We know from evidence.
Scientists model the inside of the Earth as three layers.
The crust is the thin, hard, rocky outside. We live on it.
Under it is the mantle: a very thick layer of hot, solid rock.
The mantle is most of the Earth. It is so hot that it can flow, very slowly.
At the centre is the core. It is metal, not rock.
The core is about as hot as the surface of the Sun.

at.sun: as hot as the surface of the Sun

beats.say: Under the crust, rock is so hot that it melts. Melted rock underground is magma.
Where the crust is broken, magma pushes up through the crack.
It erupts. Red-hot lava pours out, with ash and gas.
Lava is magma that has reached the surface.
The lava cools into new rock. The mountain grows, with a crater at the top.
Volcanoes are found at breaks in the crust. That is why they come in lines.
The crust is not one shell. It is broken into huge pieces called plates.
The plates rest on the hot mantle. They creep along as fast as your fingernails grow.

at.nails: as fast as your fingernails grow

beats.say: Where two plates push against each other, their edges catch and stick.
The push builds up for years. Then the edges slip, all at once.
That sudden move is an earthquake, and the ground shakes.
A crack is left behind. Earthquakes happen at the same breaks as volcanoes.
How thin is the crust, really? Imagine the Earth as an apple.
The skin stands for the crust. The real crust is even thinner.
The flesh is the mantle: most of the Earth, thick and hot.
The apple's core stands for the Earth's core, but it is far too small.
No model shows everything. This one leaves out the heat and the metal.
Nobody has seen the mantle or the core. So how do we know?
Earthquakes send waves right through the Earth. Some only travel through solids.
They pass through the mantle, so the mantle is solid.
They cannot get through the outer core, so that part is liquid.
The Earth is far too heavy to be rock all the way through.
And meteorites, rocks from space, are sometimes made of iron. The core is metal.
Evidence from enquiry built this model. It changed what people thought.
Crust, mantle, core: thin rock, thick hot rock, and metal at the centre.
Volcanoes and earthquakes happen where the crust is broken.
An apple can model that, and evidence is how we know.
